title: The continuation bet
summary: When the preflop raiser should bet the flop, and how much.

what.text: A **continuation bet** (c-bet) is a flop bet by the player who raised preflop. It works because the opponent usually misses the flop: they make a pair or better only about a third of the time. When they fold, you win the pot without a hand.

size.text:
The size depends on the texture:
- A **dry board** where you have the range advantage (K♠ 7♦ 2♣): a small c-bet of **25–33% of the pot** with almost your whole range. The opponent has little to defend with, and a cheap bet risks little.
- A **wet board** (J♥ T♥ 8♣): bet less often but bigger, **60–75% of the pot**. You charge draws and protect made hands.
- Against **several opponents**, bet less often and mostly for value: the chance that everyone folds drops a lot.

labels: Dry board, ace-queen: a small c-bet (⅓ pot)
Wet board, ace-king without a pair: check, or a big bet using the backdoor draws

when-not.text: When to skip the c-bet: the board suits the opponent's range (8♠ 7♦ 6♣ after a big blind call), there are two or more opponents and you have neither a hand nor a draw, or the opponent hardly ever folds on the flop.

q-size.q: You opened from the CO and the BB called. Flop K♠ 7♦ 2♣. Which c-bet is usually better?
q-size.explain: A dry king-high board favors the raiser: a small c-bet with almost the whole range.

options: Any player who bets the flop first
t1.explain: A c-bet continues the preflop raise with the same aggression on the flop.

t2.q: Flop J♥ T♥ 8♣. Which c-bet approach is more sensible?
options: A small bet with the whole range
t2.explain: A wet board is full of draws: a big bet charges them, and weak hands are better off checking.

t3.q: Why does a bluff c-bet work worse against three opponents?
options: It is unlikely that all of them fold
t3.explain: Each opponent can hit the flop, and the chance that all three fold is small.
